cards.title: Does the n/2-Ramsey search problem belong to TFAP?
cards.formal: Does the total search problem that, given adjacency-query access to a simple graph on 2^n vertices, asks for a clique or an independent set of size ⌊n/2⌋ belong to TFAP in the source’s black-box sense, namely the closure of robust total search problems under low-depth decision-tree many-one reductions?
cards.why: Would clarify whether Ramsey totality has the robustness underlying abundant-solution search classes, and sharpen the relationship between Ramsey search and pigeonhole-based TFNP principles.

references.title: Total NP Search Problems with Abundant Solutions

cards.definitions: Take n≥4, vertex set {0,1}^n and one input bit for each unordered pair of distinct vertices; let N=binom(2^n,2) be the number of these bits. A solution lists ⌊n/2⌋ distinct vertices and identifies whether all pairs are edges or all are nonedges. Each solution can be verified with O(n²)=poly(log N) queries. A black-box TFNP problem is a family R_N⊆{0,1}^N×O_N, with finite solution sets O_N, total on every input, and with a decision tree of depth poly(log N) verifying each proposed solution. A partial input a∈{0,1,*}^N is witnessing if some one output o is valid for every complete input extending a. A function h(N) is negligible in log N when, for every constant c>0, h(N)≤(log N)^{-c} for all sufficiently large N. A problem is robust if for every such nonnegative h, all sufficiently large N have the property that every partial input fixing at least (1−h(N))N bits is witnessing. A deterministic decision-tree many-one reduction R_N→Q_M has one depth-poly(log N) tree computing each target input bit and, for every target solution o, one such tree decoding a source solution; log M is poly(log N). For every source input x and every valid target solution o of the constructed target, decoding must give a valid source solution. No uniform circuit-construction condition is imposed on these decision trees. TFAP^dt consists precisely of problems reducible in this sense to a robust black-box TFNP problem. The source’s circuit-input TFAP definition assigns membership through this oracle counterpart: an explicit succinct adjacency circuit does not authorize a stronger, arbitrary white-box reduction. The floor fixes the harmless integer convention for the source’s n/2 notation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a low-depth decision-tree many-one reduction from this Ramsey search family to a robust total search family, with the required target-size bound and correctness for every target solution, or prove that no such reduction exists. Showing merely that every graph has many Ramsey sets, or proving membership for the smaller n/10 target, does not resolve this membership question.

context_blocks.title: The graph is exponentially larger than a requested solution
context_blocks.text: The input describes 2^n vertices, but an answer contains only about n/2 of them. Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of that size in every graph. Checking a proposed answer needs only its pairwise adjacency bits.

context_blocks.title: Abundance means resilience of totality
context_blocks.text: A robust problem still has one definite valid answer after almost all input bits have been fixed, regardless of how the few missing bits are completed. This is stronger than counting many answers on each complete input: different completions could have entirely different valid sets.

context_blocks.title: The Ramsey relation itself need not be robust
context_blocks.text: TFAP includes reductions to robust problems. Membership can therefore hold without proving that this particular adjacency-bit presentation has the robustness property. The reduction must preserve validity for every solution returned by the target.

context_blocks.title: Why this class matters
context_blocks.text: The source places weak pigeonhole search and several other abundant-solution tasks in TFAP and proves black-box separations from several standard TFNP subclasses. It conjectures Ramsey membership as a way to locate its totality principle more precisely.

context_blocks.title: The smaller target is a separate question
context_blocks.text: The source asks about n/10-Ramsey if n/2-Ramsey is not in TFAP. Finding a set of size n/10 is easier as an output requirement, so membership of that variant would not establish membership for the larger set requested here.

cards.title: Does W[1] ≠ FPT imply the Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis?
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Assuming W[1]≠FPT, is there an absolute constant ε∈(0,1) such that no deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm can distinguish a satisfiable binary constraint satisfaction instance on k variables from an instance in which every assignment violates at least an ε fraction of the constraints, with k as the parameter?
cards.why: Would supply a parameterized analogue of the PCP theorem from the standard exact-hardness assumption, giving a common basis for constant-gap inapproximability across many parameterized optimization problems.
cards.status_note: Source definitions, the ETH theorem and the February 2026 survey checked with later-result searches through 12 September 2026. No proof under only W[1]≠FPT was located.

progress.text: Baby PIH is established under W[1]≠FPT; the full PIH implication is left open.
The journal version of PIH under ETH records the stronger-assumption theorem, whose preprint already appeared in 2023.
The survey explicitly retains the distinction between PIH under ETH and PIH under W[1]≠FPT.

references.authors: Guruswami, Venkatesan; Ren, Xuandi; Sandeep, Sai

cards.definitions: A binary constraint satisfaction instance has k variables, a finite alphabet Σ of size n, and explicitly given binary relations specifying the allowed pairs for constrained variable pairs. Its finite input length includes these relation tables. An assignment chooses one alphabet value for each variable; val(Π) is the maximum fraction of its constraints satisfied by an assignment. The promise is val(Π)=1 or val(Π)≤1−ε; no answer is prescribed for intermediate values. For an instance of encoded size L, fixed-parameter tractable means time f(k)L^C for some computable f and constant C independent of k and L. In the standard representation with one binary relation per constrained pair, this is equivalent to f(k)n^{O(1)} after absorbing polynomial k-factors into f. Here W[1]≠FPT is the standard deterministic hypothesis, equivalently that deciding whether a finite graph has a k-clique has no f(k)L^C algorithm. PIH asserts the existence of one fixed ε>0 for which the promised approximation task has no such algorithm, irrespective of the computable function f or constant exponent C. The question is the implication from exact parameterized hardness to that constant-gap hardness, not an unconditional assertion of W[1]≠FPT.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated implication using only W[1]≠FPT as the complexity assumption, with a constant gap independent of k and n, or refute that implication. A result assuming ETH or Gap-ETH, a gap shrinking with k, or hardness for a list-assignment variant does not settle this target.

context_blocks.title: Finding one violated constraint is weaker than finding many
context_blocks.text: Exact unsatisfiability only says every assignment fails somewhere. PIH asks for a constant fraction of failures on every assignment. If an instance has many constraints, the existence of just one unavoidable violation need not give any fixed gap.

context_blocks.title: The parameter is the number of variables
context_blocks.text: The alphabet is allowed to grow with the input. Exhaustive search takes n^k time, whose exponent depends on k; that is not fixed-parameter tractable. A running time such as 2^{2^k}n^3 would qualify despite its very large dependence on k.

context_blocks.title: The source proves Baby PIH under the desired assumption
context_blocks.text: Baby PIH distinguishes satisfiable instances from instances for which even a constant-size list of values at each variable cannot satisfy every constraint. This is a different guarantee from saying that every ordinary assignment violates a constant fraction of constraints.

context_blocks.title: ETH already implies PIH
context_blocks.text: The Guruswami–Lin–Ren–Sun–Wu theorem derives PIH from the Exponential Time Hypothesis. ETH imposes a quantitative subexponential-time obstruction for 3SAT and is a stronger assumption than the parameterized separation sought here. The February 2026 survey still separates these targets.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
